hints: Dynamic `import()` of a `file://` URL works for `.mjs`; `require()` of an absolute `.cjs` path works from a CommonJS script — write both temp files with `fs.writeFileSync` into `os.tmpdir()`.
The namespace object returned by `await import(...)` exposes live bindings as properties — read `ns.count` AFTER calling `ns.bump()`.
Wrap the script in an async IIFE so you can use `await` in a plain `.js` file, and delete the temp dir with `fs.rmSync` when done.
exercises.prompt:
Prove the live-binding difference between ESM and CommonJS with a self-contained Node script.

Your script must:

- Write two temporary module files into `os.tmpdir()`: `counter.mjs` (ESM — `export let count = 0;` plus an exported `bump()` that increments it) and `counter.cjs` (CommonJS — a module-local `let count = 0;`, a `bump()` function, and `module.exports = { count, bump };` which snapshots the value at load time).
- Dynamically `import()` the `.mjs` file, call its `bump()`, then read the exported `count` through the namespace object.
- `require()` the `.cjs` file, call its `bump()`, then read the exported `count`.
- Print exactly the lines below, then delete the temp files.

The ESM read must print `1` (live binding — the importer's view tracks the exporter's variable); the CJS read must print `0` (snapshot — the primitive was copied into `module.exports` when the module loaded). Use only `node:fs`, `node:os`, `node:path` (dynamic `import()` needs no import).

Example:
```js
// node live-bindings.js
```
Expected output:
```
esm.count after bump: 1
cjs.count after bump: 0
```
exercises.title: Live bindings, proven in Node

hints: Detect the opaque shape with regexes for `module.exports =` and `export default {` — either one forces `false`.
For the named shape, check three things: the module declares `export function mul` (or const/let/class), the consumer has a static `import { ... } from`, and that import list does not name `mul`.
Keep the two module/consumer pairs as plain strings — you're analyzing source text, not executing the modules.
exercises.prompt:
Bundlers can only tree-shake what they can statically analyze. Write a script that models a bundler's static analysis as a `canDropUnused(moduleSrc, consumerSrc, unusedName)` function:

- If the module uses an opaque object export (`module.exports = {...}` or `export default {...}`), the bundler cannot statically enumerate the exports — return `false` (it must keep everything).
- If the module uses ESM **named** exports and the consumer uses a static `import { ... }` that does not include the unused name, the bundler can prove the export is unused — return `true`.

Apply it to both shapes below (a CommonJS object-export module and an ESM named-export module, each with a consumer that only uses `add`) and print the verdicts.

Example:
```js
// node shake-check.js
```
Expected output:
```
object-export shape:  can drop unused 'mul'? false
named-export shape:   can drop unused 'mul'? true
```
exercises.title: Refactor for tree-shaking

hints: The generator body is an infinite `while (true)` loop — it never terminates on its own; `yield` pauses it and `take` stops asking.
Destructure-swap `let [a, b] = [0, 1]` then `[a, b] = [b, a + b]` after each yield to advance the sequence.
`take` can use `for...of` directly on the generator (generators are iterable) and `break` once it has `n` values.

hints: Recurse: when `path` is empty, return `value`; otherwise shallow-copy the current level, then set `clone[key] = setIn(obj[key], rest, value)`.
Choose the copy by type — `Array.isArray(base) ? base.slice() : { ...base }` — so array indices work as path segments.
Untouched branches are shared automatically: you only ever copy objects that lie on the path.

lessons.comparisonNote: Java's `import` is a compile-time namespace alias — the class and its static fields live in one place, and every reader sees the current value. ESM live bindings behave the same way (read through the binding, see the current value). CommonJS destructuring is the odd one out: it's like copying a static field's value into a local at class-load time and never looking at the field again.
keyPoints: CommonJS (`require`/`module.exports`) is Node's 2009 synchronous system; ESM (`import`/`export`) is the ES2015 standard and the default for new code.
ESM imports are live bindings to the exporter's variables; CommonJS destructuring at require time copies primitive values (a snapshot).
ESM tolerates circular imports via hoisted bindings (TDZ errors on early reads); CommonJS hands back a partially populated exports object.
Interop: ESM can import CJS (default import = module.exports), but CJS cannot require() ESM — use dynamic import(); __dirname doesn't exist in ESM.
lessons.title: ESM vs CommonJS: Syntax, Live Bindings, and Interop

lessons.comparisonNote: The JVM world has the same optimization under a different name: ProGuard/R8 tree-shake Android apps by stripping unreachable methods from the whole program. And `sideEffects: false` plays the role of a purity contract — the bundler trusts your annotation the way a JIT trusts that a method you marked side-effect-free won't surprise it.
keyPoints: Tree-shaking drops unused exports, but only when the bundler can statically resolve them — ESM named exports shake, `module.exports = {...}` and default-exported objects don't.
Ship libraries as ESM with per-function named exports if you want consumers' bundlers to shake them.
`sideEffects: false` in package.json lets the bundler drop unused modules entirely; list files with import-time side effects (CSS, polyfills) explicitly.
Mis-marking side effects is a silent production bug: the bundler deletes code it was told was safe to delete.
lessons.title: What Bundlers Actually Do: Tree-Shaking and sideEffects

lessons.comparisonNote: `user?.address?.city ?? 'unknown'` is Java's `Optional.ofNullable(user).map(User::getAddress).map(Address::getCity).orElse("unknown")` without the ceremony. And spread-copy updates mirror how you'd build a modified copy of a Java record — construct a new value with one field changed, never mutate the original.
keyPoints: `...` spreads when expanding and rests when collecting — position determines the job.
`??` falls through only on null/undefined; `||` also falls through on 0, '', and false — use `??` when those are legitimate values.
Update immutably: map/filter for arrays, spread-copy each level of a nested path, structuredClone for true deep copies.
Copying the path (not deep-cloning) preserves reference identity for untouched branches — that's what memoization relies on.
lessons.title: Modern Idioms: Destructuring, Spread, and Immutability

lessons.comparisonNote: Think of a generator as Java's `Iterator` fused with a lazy `Stream`: `Stream.iterate(0, n -> n + 1)` captures the same 'infinite values on demand' idea, and each `yield` is like a `tryAdvance` that suspends the method mid-execution instead of returning.
keyPoints: The iteration protocol is `[Symbol.iterator]()` returning `{ next() }`; for...of, spread, and destructuring all consume it.
Generators (`function*`/`yield`) pause execution — nothing runs until `.next()` is called, enabling lazy infinite sequences.
Use them for lazy sequences, custom iterable data structures, and `yield*` composition.
async/await is built on generators — 'pause here, resume later' is the model behind every async abstraction.
lessons.title: Iterators, Generators, and Lazy Sequences
